findings.title: Plaintext recovery codes sent to user storage providers
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw plaintext recovery codes to JSON and passes them to the user storage provider through updateCredential. Locally created recovery codes are stored hashed, so any federated provider now receives and may persist the codes in cleartext. A leak of the external store would directly expose usable second-factor codes.

findings.title: Used recovery codes are never consumed in user storage
findings.body: When the credential comes from the federated provider, removeStoredCredentialById only deletes local DB credentials. Nothing else in the flow marks a used code as consumed in the federated store. As a result the same recovery code stays valid indefinitely, and the 'next code' number in the login bean never advances. Recovery codes are meant to be single-use, so this defeats that guarantee for user-storage users.

findings.title: Federated credential always preferred over local, even if stale
findings.body: getCredential prefers federated credentials and only falls back to local storage if none are found. If a user has both a local credential and a federated one, the local credential is ignored. That can show the wrong code number to the user or skip the all-codes-used handling for the credential that is actually being validated.

findings.title: Unchecked Optional.get on recovery code credential
findings.body: credentialModelOpt.get() is called without checking the Optional. If neither user storage nor the local DB returns a recovery-codes credential, for example when the provider's isConfiguredFor and getCredentials disagree, this throws NoSuchElementException and the login page fails to render.
